items.title: [Théoo] My phone is a noisy place
items.content_html:
A while back, I shared a note about how I had cut down my phone usage a lot and what it had changed for me.

And for a few months, I actually stuck to it.
But lately, I've been watching or listening to videos from the moment I wake up to the moment I go to sleep. And for the times when I can't watch videos (like when I'm walking in the street, for example), I will put a podcast or music to occupy the space.

I'm not sure why I went back to this sluggish state when I had been doing so well for a long time, but I think it's because I actually missed watching specific YouTubers and listening to specific podcasts. So I allowed some back into my life and then some more and eventually, it took over.

Which leaves me in a weird situation, because I now know that no YouTube at all is disappointing. There is some content that I actually like and don't want to stop watching, especially since it's only like at most 2 hours per week plus the occasional GeoWizard adventure.
But at the same time, I know that if I let these back in, I won't be able to stop myself, because there is a ton of content that I like, content that I wouldn't miss if I didn't watch it, but that is still nice to watch.
I could try an extension to hide the recommendations, but knowing me, I will probably deactivate it pretty quickly and find an "acceptable" reason why. Worth a try though, I guess.

The other thing that crept back is Spotify. I listen to music (or podcasts, but mostly music) when I'm not watching videos. On the one hand, it's great because I have discovered many new artists lately, but at the same time, I've been feeling more disconnected, irritated when someone is trying to talk to me and I have to remove my AirPods and, overall like my mind can never breathe.
I'd say that the thing that has changed since the last article is that now silence isn't weird anymore. I even enjoy it! But for some reason I always feel this need to listen to something. Plus, I have been questioning my relationship with music lately, but I will talk about it in another note.

Now again, I'm not sure about what the right thing to do is. I definitely don't want to stop listening to music, I enjoy it way too much. But I don't want it to be constant.
Trying to apply time restrictions won't work because I know that I will find "good reasons" to circumvent them.
Maybe something like "you can only listen to music when you do this and that" could work. This has worked for podcasts already, as there are some podcasts that I only listen to when cleaning and others I only listen to when grocery shopping.
Another idea would be to say "You can only listen to music out loud" and not in your AirPods. So that would automatically limit my time, because there are many situations where you can't listen to music out loud.

So where does this leave me? What about the things I said in the previous note about enjoying life without all this?
I guess it's as with all things in life, I need to find balance.

The approach to ditch all music and YouTube was certainly too extreme, but spending my whole days listening to stuff is also too extreme.
Another thing to consider is the fact that I tend to get absorbed by things, both the good and the bad ones.
So when I get to reading a book or programming something, I will just do it for hours upon hours to the point of forgetting to eat. But the same can be said for playing video games and watching videos, which has a much more negative impact.
And I don't know that I should change this, it's just a part of my personality, but I need to learn to put systems in place to prevent it for things that make me rot away.

I don't have a good conclusion yet. Honestly, I think that what would help me would be to have the opinions from a bunch of different people and see how they deal with all this, to try as many options as possible until I find the balance I'm looking for.

For now, I will try to limit Spotify and I will try YouTube "blocking" extensions. If you have any other ideas or want to share your experience, please email me, I'd be grateful to receive it.

I hope you have a great day, bye.

items.title: [Pinterest Engineering Blog - Medium] How Pinterest Improved Analytics Agent Compliance with Loop Engineering
items.content_html:
Skyler Zheng | Software Engineer II; Chris Moradi | Staff Data Scientist; Lu Liu | Staff Software Engineer; Aman Gairola | Manager II; Michael Chau | Manager II

The Compliance Problem

Compliance means following the right steps at the right time

Pinterest’s Analytics Agent helps teams answer questions such as “How did query latency for the ads reporting pipeline change last week?” It searches the company’s data ecosystem, analyzes the relevant information, and recommends an answer or course of action.

Not every question requires the same steps. We call the agent compliant when it identifies and follows the steps that apply. Improving compliance is intended to make answers more consistent and reduce the risk of incomplete or inaccurate results. Examples include:

  • Read the data-discovery skill when it needs help finding the right tools or sources.
  • Inspect table metadata before writing SQL to learn what the columns mean, which filters are required, and whether the table has important usage notes.
  • Search every relevant source type, including tables, dashboards, and metrics, rather than stopping at the first useful result.

These are three examples from a broader set of compliance rules, and whether they apply depends on the question. If a user provides the appropriate table, the agent may not need the data-discovery skill, while an open-ended question may require a broader search. The agent must decide which rules apply and follow them when needed.

That flexibility also makes compliance difficult. When the agent skips a required step, it may stop at the first table it finds, miss an important filter in the metadata, or overlook a certified metric with a more authoritative definition. It could then confidently report that “latency is down 4.2%.”[1] The answer may sound reasonable while using the wrong definition, pipeline stage, or reporting window.

Why manually revising the agent’s instructions was not enough

Measuring noncompliance showed us where the agent failed, but not how to fix it. After parsing existing chat logs, we found that table searches occurred more than ten times as often as chart and dashboard searches.[2] For a separate rule requiring the agent to read the data-discovery skill, compliance reached only 64% across a broader set of chats even after we manually revised the agent’s instructions.[3]

It was often difficult to predict which change would improve the agent because the model could interpret reasonable instructions in unexpected ways. One guardrail designed to keep the agent within its intended scope seemed reasonable:

Scope: Only answer questions within your domain. For unrelated requests, politely decline and suggest that the user try a general-purpose assistant.

The guardrail produced an unexpected response:

User, paraphrased: “What are the cloud storage costs for this table, and how long is its data retained?”

Agent, paraphrased: “This is outside my domain. Please try a general-purpose assistant.”

Although the topic sounded like specialized infrastructure, it was an in-scope data question because the agent had access to relevant storage data. The agent had misclassified the question and declined without searching. We identified the cause only after trying and evaluating several changes.

Manually revising the agent’s instructions therefore became a process of trial and error, with no reliable way to know whether a change would generalize or break something else. We needed a repeatable process that could propose a change, test it, and use the results to guide the next attempt. That cycle of proposing, testing, and learning became the foundation of what we call loop engineering. We explain the full approach later in this article. Before building it, however, we first needed test suites that defined success and protected behavior that already worked.

Build the Evaluation Framework

Start with paired test suites

We built a separate pair of test suites for each compliance rule we wanted to improve, such as reading the data-discovery skill or searching all required source types. A focused LLM labeler answered two questions for each chat, and humans reviewed the labels:

  1. Does this compliance rule apply to this chat?
  2. If it applies, did the agent follow this compliance rule?

We used the first answer to assign each chat to a suite. If the rule applied, the chat went into the required suite. If it did not, the chat went into the skip suite. We then compared the agent’s behavior with that expectation. A chat passed if the agent followed the rule when required or skipped it when it was not needed. These pass and fail labels gave us a baseline for comparing future versions.

Both suites are necessary. If we tested only required cases, a system prompt telling the agent to “always search dashboards” could earn a perfect score even when a dashboard was irrelevant. We saw this tradeoff in testing. A change that made the agent search dashboards more aggressively fixed one chat where a dashboard was required, but it also triggered dashboard searches in two chats where they were not. The required suite showed the improvement; only the skip suite revealed the two new regressions.[2]

Together, the suites gave the loop a balanced goal: follow the rule when a question requires it, and avoid unnecessary actions when it does not.

Protect unrelated behavior with regression tests

These two suites covered only the rule we were tuning. We also needed to protect everything else the agent already did well. For that, we used a much larger regression suite and rejected any change that pushed its performance below the required level.

Once we could measure progress, the next challenge was helping each iteration learn from the ones before it.

Design the Tuning Loop

Why persistent sessions and Ralph Wiggum loops both fell short

Our first design kept one agent session open across every iteration. The full history helped the agent make better decisions early, but the context grew with every attempt. Later iterations became more expensive and less reliable.

The second design used a memoryless pattern often called a Ralph Wiggum loop. Every iteration started with a fresh context window, reducing the context sent to the model and lowering the estimated model cost by about fivefold.[4] The tradeoff was that it often repeated earlier mistakes because it had no memory of what had already failed.

One design remembered too much; the other remembered nothing. The final design needed fresh context without losing the lessons from earlier iterations.

Fresh context with structured memory

Every iteration now starts a fresh session and reads a compact, structured handoff. The handoff records:

  • Current results: Scores for every test suite, including validation cases not used for tuning.
  • What is failing: The cases that still fail and their likely causes, helping the agent address a broader pattern instead of one example at a time.
  • The best change so far: The highest-performing change from earlier iterations, which becomes the starting point for the next one.
  • What not to repeat: Previous approaches that reduced performance or failed to solve the problem.
  • Possible test problems: Cases that no candidate has passed, which may indicate an issue with the test rather than the agent.
  • What must remain stable: Test suites that are not allowed to regress, along with the file and line limits for the next change.

The handoff preserves decisions rather than conversation history. Each new session receives the evidence it needs, while the context stays small enough to remain useful.

How the tuning loop works

For each rule, we split the required and skip cases into tuning and validation sets. The tuning cases guide improvements to the agent, while the validation cases test those improvements on examples that did not guide them. A final holdout set stays untouched until the end. Alongside these rule-specific cases, the larger regression suite checks that the agent’s other capabilities still work.

Each iteration follows the same process:

  1. Draft up to four changes to the Analytics Agent’s system prompt, skills, context layer, or tools.
  2. Evaluate every candidate on the same small sample and select the highest-scoring one. If the scores are effectively tied, prefer the change that adds less prompt context and modifies fewer lines.
  3. Evaluate the winner on the full tuning and validation suites.
  4. Apply the acceptance checks, then keep or revert the change.

The loop repeats until it reaches its targets, with a preset budget serving as a safety limit. When the run ends, it evaluates the final result on the holdout set.

Reject changes that improve the wrong thing

A higher tuning score is not enough to keep a change. It must also pass three independent safety checks:

  • Repair/break gate: Did the change fix more cases than it broke?
  • Acceptance critic: Does the change address a general pattern, or does it hard-code an answer from the test set?
  • Regression guard: Did the change reduce performance on a test suite that was not allowed to regress?

The checks make acceptance deliberately conservative. A higher score is not useful if the change overfits the test cases or damages another capability.

We also limit what the loop can change. Each proposal may modify only the agent’s system prompt, skills, context layer, and tools. It is capped at a few files and a few dozen lines, with the limit shrinking over the run. Changes outside those boundaries are reverted. This prevents the loop from modifying application code to make its own tests easier to pass.

The shrinking limit also favors small, targeted changes over unnecessary rewrites. Without that constraint, an agent may rewrite a prompt that already works. Amazon’s Promptimus reports the same tendency in its edit mode.

Measure Real Improvement

The run that fooled us

With the test architecture and safety checks in place, the design appeared ready. Our first large run reached 89.3% compliance across its tuning and validation cases.[4] The iteration history told a less impressive story. Most of the gain came from the first accepted change, and iterations 21 through 30 added nothing.

The plateau raised a more fundamental question: when a score moved by one or two cases, was the change real or simply normal model variation?

Despite similar totals, 10.3% of cases changed verdict between runs.[2] Because gains and losses nearly canceled each other out, the aggregate score hid substantial case-level variation.

Learn from individual cases, not only the score

Evaluating every candidate on all 223 cases would take too long, so we first run each one on the same sample of about a dozen cases. With a 10% flip rate, roughly one result in a sample that size may change by chance. That is why we do not rely on a small score increase alone.

The overall score tells us whether performance moved, but individual cases tell us what changed. The loop records which cases changed from fail to pass and which changed from pass to fail. The next iteration uses those results to identify what improved, what broke, and what to address next. Validation cases and the broader regression suite provide additional evidence before the loop accepts a change.

Results: small changes backed by strong evidence

The loop improved compliance in chats where each rule was needed while preserving performance in the skip and regression suites.[3] In other words, a change had to fix existing failures without breaking cases the agent already handled correctly.

The improvement in searching every relevant source type came from a backend change to the Analytics Agent’s search process. Reaching it required two labeled datasets, a dozen loop iterations, and two verification runs. Most of the work went into identifying a change that improved compliance without introducing regressions.

From Prompt Engineering to Loop Engineering

The Analytics Agent now interprets experiment results, respects restricted-data access, builds dashboards, writes reports, and continues to take on new responsibilities. As these capabilities expand, a change intended to improve one workflow can affect how the agent handles others, sometimes introducing new failures.

That is why we moved from one-off instruction changes to loop engineering. People define the goals, evaluation criteria, and safety boundaries. The loop proposes changes, tests them against real failures, and rejects those that introduce regressions. The same process can target other goals, including consistency, latency, and accuracy, as the agent evolves.

Loop engineering turns failures from real user chats into tests that guide changes to the agent. By keeping only changes that improve compliance without damaging existing behavior, it gives us a repeatable way to make answers more reliable as the Analytics Agent evolves.

Acknowledgements

None of this would have been possible without the people who shaped and supported this work. We thank Attila Dobi for design reviews that strengthened the loop; Jason Coffman for the Analytics Agent capabilities and infrastructure; Bryant Xiao for sponsorship and engineering guidance; Yi Wu and Laura Palmer for product vision and direction; and J.C. Zhong, Yufei Dong for the real-world evaluation data and infrastructure.

Footnotes

[1] Illustrative example; not actual Pinterest data.

[2] Pinterest internal evaluation data, global, July to September 2026. Search figures count tool calls, not successful retrieval. One trial per case, and the LLM labeler is not calibrated against human labels. All runs used one base model at one reasoning setting (Claude 4.7 Opus Fast), so results may not hold across models.

[3] Same source as [2]. The 64% figure is the compliance rate across a broader population after the agent’s instructions were manually revised; it is not a before-and-after comparison. The skill-read suite was a separate 41-case dataset built entirely from known failures, so its baseline was 0% by design. The expected-benefit column describes what we expect each rule to improve; we have not measured answer quality directly.

[4] Same source as [2]. The 89.3% is a pooled pass rate over the run’s tuning and validation cases, with most of the gain landing at the first change and nothing kept after iteration 20. The cost comparison is an internal estimate of model inference cost, not a controlled benchmark.

How Pinterest Improved Analytics Agent Compliance with Loop Engineering was originally published in Pinterest Engineering Blog on Medium, where people are continuing the conversation by highlighting and responding to this story.

items.title: [healio.com] US cancer society urges PSA screening from age 50
items.content_html: The American Cancer Society has issued its first prostate cancer screening update since 2010, recommending prostate-specific antigen (PSA) blood tests every two years for men at average risk ages 50 to 69. It recommends annual screening starting at age 45 for Black men and men with a strong family history. Men with one non-Black first-degree relative diagnosed at age 65 or older should start screening at 45 and test every two years. The guidance shifts from primarily advising average-risk men to discuss screening with a clinician, while retaining informed discussions of potential benefits and harms. For men ages 70 to 74, screening decisions should reflect health and prior PSA results. Screening is not recommended for those age 80 or older or people unlikely to live another 10 years. To limit false alarms and treatment of slow-growing tumors, the society recommends confirming elevated PSA results and using MRI or biomarkers to help decide whether a biopsy is needed. Low-risk cancers may be monitored. The society cited long-term European trial data showing screening was associated with a 13% lower risk of death from prostate cancer.

items.title: [news-medical.net] Review finds type 2 diabetes tied to 53% higher Alzheimer’s risk
items.content_html: A review of 40 studies found that people with type 2 diabetes had a 53% higher adjusted relative risk of Alzheimer’s disease than those without diabetes. It estimated 4.7 new Alzheimer’s cases per 1,000 people with type 2 diabetes each year. A separate study of 400 adults found that two inflammation measures derived from blood counts varied across glycemic groups defined by HbA1c, but their clinical usefulness remains unestablished. Other research linked higher preoperative HbA1c to more recorded nonunion diagnoses after cervical spine fusion, while a mouse experiment found that parathyroid hormone treatments restored some diabetes-related jawbone loss. The surgery study was observational and did not establish causation or a threshold for delaying surgery; the jawbone findings have not established a treatment effect in people.

items.title: [lakartidningen.se] Swedish doctors call for stricter checks after AI misses drug interaction
items.content_html: Swedish doctors are urging stronger safety testing and oversight of clinical artificial intelligence after a decision-support tool failed to flag a potential interaction between clindamycin and carbamazepine, an epilepsy medicine. The omission blocked the system’s launch; the case was later added to recurring tests, including checks after system updates. The doctors say clinical AI developers should ensure answers draw on reliable sources and include critical safety information, while healthcare providers should require proper certification and ongoing risk monitoring. Separately, an opinion article in JAMA co-signed by a former U.S. Food and Drug Administration commissioner warns that betting on clinical-trial outcomes can create incentives that threaten trial blinding, participant retention and research integrity.

items.title: [mobihealthnews.com] Studies find medical AI speeds some diagnoses but accuracy varies
items.content_html: Three studies found that artificial intelligence (AI) can assist diagnosis, but results varied by task. In a South Korean ear-disease study, junior residents’ accuracy rose from 54.4% to 86.6% with AI support; in a rheumatology trial, an AI tool cut case-processing time from 206 seconds to 94 seconds but did not significantly improve diagnostic accuracy. In a retrospective study of emergency-department notes, a language model outperformed a benchmark model in confirming suspected stroke diagnoses, but researchers said it needs validation at independent hospitals before clinical use. In the ear-disease study, doctors using AI changed 46 initially correct diagnoses to incorrect ones.

items.title: 🔓 [Fast Company] Dads want to do more caregiving. But here’s how workplaces hold them back
items.content_html:
The tension between caregiving obligations and work responsibilities is often framed as a women’s issue. But it’s not just working mothers who find themselves in a bind: Plenty of men say they not only value caregiving but want to do more of it. So what’s holding them back?

A new report from the Better Life Lab at the think tank New America—which publishes research on workplace equity and family policy—indicates that men face some of the same hurdles that working women do, from limited flexibility or autonomy to a lack of structural support. 

Compared with 2019, men are taking more time off from work or reducing their work hours due to caregiving responsibilities, especially those who earn less or have children with special needs. At the same time, they continue to grapple with the kind of cultural stigma that can keep them from taking paid leave even when they’re entitled to it. 

The report’s findings suggest that many men actually want to spend more time on caregiving. In fact, a surprising number of fathers—6 in 10—expressed an interest in staying home full time. Men who helped care for adults or children with special needs were even more interested in being home. Over two-thirds of the men surveyed claim to think caregiving is as important as paid work, and that both parents should contribute equally. But the reality is quite different: Only about 40% of respondents who are caregivers and parents said they actually split those responsibilities equally.  

There are a number of potential explanations for this disparity. Over a quarter of dads said there are barriers to being the kind of parent they want to be, from their job to their financial situation; male caregivers of adults or children with special needs reported feeling this at similar rates. Men with higher-paying jobs—earning more than $100,000—were even more likely to report experiencing those barriers. 

As the Better Life Lab points out, however, the data seems to suggest that men are actually underreporting the extent to which work obligations actually impact their ability to show up as a parent or caregiver. 

A third of fathers said they have “no control” over their schedules; when men reported having more control over their hours, that usually meant they couldn’t dictate which days they worked, and vice versa. The majority of parents and caregivers (74%) said they would prefer to work remotely or with a hybrid arrangement if they could, but only 40% of them currently do. Whether they were parents or caregivers, only about a fifth of respondents expressed a desire to work out of an office (though men are more likely to have a preference for the office). Nearly two-thirds of fathers also said work obligations interfered with their family time. 

Perhaps the most interesting data point is that men are missing work or slashing their work hours at higher rates—a sign that men may be facing the same pressures that women have for many years. Among men who care for adults or children with special needs, the share who missed work due to care obligations rose from 64% in 2019 to 76% as of this year. About half of men also reported cutting back on their work hours, up from 42% in 2019.

As Fast Company reported recently, there has also been a noticeable shift in how men take time off when they become parents. Men are finally taking more parental leave, in part due to the rise of paid leave policies at the state level. Until recently, the data indicated that men took little time off, maybe a week at most, and often through some combination of sick days or vacation days or unpaid time off. 

But recent research shows that dads are filing just as many leave claims as moms in states like California, Colorado, and Washington, which have robust paid leave programs. In states that have had these programs for many years, leave claims from men have only increased, while states that introduced paid leave more recently have seen higher uptake from the start. 

In other words, it seems clear that when men have good access to paid leave, they’re more likely to take it—a pattern that also lines up with the Better Life Lab’s findings on how workplace culture can shape the caregiver experience. When fathers took leave, they overwhelmingly cited a supportive workplace as a reason (72%); many also pointed to a paid leave policy through their employer or state (63%). 

Still, even as men say they want to be more present, it is still women who bear the greatest burden of caregiving strain. Women are more likely to sacrifice their careers due to caregiving responsibilities, and this happens at higher rates when they are mothers. As the report’s findings suggest, women are also more quick to self-identify as caregivers and place more value on care work. 

While the culture around caregiving has shifted to some degree—especially with more men now taking leave and stepping up to care for aging parents—it’s clear that both men and women aren’t happy with the status quo.

items.title: [scimex.org] Study finds BMI misses obesity cases, misclassifies others across four countries
items.content_html: An international study of 844,108 adults in China, the United Kingdom, the United States and Spain found that using body measurements alongside body mass index (BMI) to diagnose obesity identified 3.3% to 7.4% more cases than BMI alone. The researchers tested a framework proposed by a Lancet commission in 2025 that adds measures such as waist circumference and distinguishes clinical obesity, in which excess fat impairs bodily function, from preclinical obesity, in which it poses a risk without current dysfunction. Compared with the expanded framework, BMI alone overestimated obesity in 1.2% to 3.1% of participants and missed it in 5.2% to 8.6%. Clinical obesity was associated with a 69% higher risk of death than no obesity, while 77% to 91% of people with preclinical obesity did not progress to the clinical form within 10 years. Researchers and clinicians said the added assessments could help target care, but require more detailed evaluation than BMI measurement alone.

items.title: [medical.nikkeibp.co.jp] Studies link frailty, cancer and weight to dementia outcomes
items.content_html: Three studies examined links between dementia, survival and frailty. Cancer patients with dementia had higher cancer-specific and overall mortality than matched cancer patients without dementia, while people who were overweight or obese at dementia diagnosis had lower subsequent mortality than those of normal weight. Separately, frailty predicted later dementia and disability among older adults with arthritis. The studies examined distinct populations and did not establish whether weight changes or frailty interventions alter outcomes. Researchers in the weight study said the association is not a reason for patients with dementia to try to gain weight. The cancer study used Denmark’s national cancer registry, and its findings appeared online Sept. 29 in The Lancet Healthy Longevity.

items.title: [medicaldaily.com] Stopping statins at 70 or older met trial’s safety test, but events rose
items.content_html: A trial of 1,880 adults aged 70 and older found that stopping statins prescribed to prevent a first cardiovascular event met the trial’s two-year criterion for noninferiority to continued treatment. But heart attacks, strokes or deaths occurred in 12.7% of participants who stopped, compared with 9.2% who continued, so the results do not support a general recommendation to discontinue statins. Participants had no prior cardiovascular event and at least two chronic conditions. Researchers randomly assigned them to stop or continue their medication at 24 centers in Switzerland, France and the Netherlands. The findings were presented Nov. 7 at the American Heart Association’s Scientific Sessions in Chicago and published in The New England Journal of Medicine.

items.title: [ScienceDaily] Alzheimer’s may have early warning signs outside the brain
items.content_html: A surprising discovery suggests that some early signs of Alzheimer’s disease may begin outside the brain. Using miniature laboratory systems made from human cells, scientists found that genetic mutations associated with inherited Alzheimer’s can disrupt nerve-to-muscle connections without any involvement from the brain or spinal cord. This could help explain why some patients experience changes in balance, walking, and coordination long before memory problems develop.

items.title: [sci.news] Peruvian fossil reveals pygmy sperm whale with extreme skull asymmetry
items.content_html: Researchers have described Scaphokogia huachafo, an extinct pygmy sperm whale whose fossil skull shows the most extreme facial asymmetry documented in a cetacean, and possibly in any mammal. The animal lived in what is now southern Peru between 6.3 million and 5.6 million years ago and was about 2.7 meters long. Both bony nostrils sat on the left side of its skull. Its dense, downward-curving snout and flexible neck suggest it searched for food in shallow seabed sediments. Researchers propose that it used echolocation to locate buried prey; unlike some bottom-feeding marine mammals, it had no facial whiskers or other specialized sensory structures for foraging.

items.title: [scitechdaily.com] Stanford researchers use brain scans to flag Alzheimer’s risk years earlier
items.content_html: Stanford Medicine researchers developed an MRI-based score that identified brain activity patterns linked to later cognitive decline and Alzheimer’s disease, potentially before memory problems or established biomarkers appear. The researchers developed the Alzheimer’s resilience-vulnerability connectome (ARC) score by comparing brain scans taken at rest from 180 adults over 75 with unusually strong memory and 110 people diagnosed with Alzheimer’s. They then tested it in more than 1,300 cognitively healthy adults aged 55 to 70. During up to 12 years of follow-up, participants with more Alzheimer’s-like patterns experienced faster cognitive decline and were more likely to develop amyloid plaques or receive a diagnosis. The researchers say the score is neither a diagnosis nor a certain prediction for an individual. They are planning a trial to test whether cognitive training can change ARC scores.

items.title: [newspaceeconomy.ca] Researchers test AI systems for satellite servicing, imaging and astronomy
items.content_html: Three research efforts are testing autonomous decision-making for space operations, from analyzing Earth imagery in orbit to guiding satellite rescues and scheduling astronomical observations. Planet Labs’ Pelican-4 satellite used an onboard NVIDIA Jetson Orin processor to detect aircraft in imagery in March. Google Research and Planet Labs said a prototype later ran the Gemma 4 model on an orbital tensor-processing unit. A team led by the University of Illinois Urbana-Champaign is developing CORTEX, software to plan and guide a servicing spacecraft’s approach to an unresponsive satellite. A separate astronomical-survey challenge evaluated systems submitted by 102 teams in simulated observing campaigns. Researchers found that leading entries combined numerical exposure planning with language models, while changes to science priorities substantially changed the systems’ rankings.
